props.title: Rhapsody in Blue
props.initialSlug: Musical portrait of George Gershwin's rise to fame

sections.content: Rhapsody in Blue stands as Warner Bros' ambitious attempt to capture George Gershwin's meteoric rise in American music through Hollywood's glossy biographical lens. Robert Alda portrays Gershwin in this heavily romanticized but visually striking film that follows similar patterns to other musician biopics like Night and Day (1946) about Cole Porter. The film's most memorable sequences center on the creation and first performance of "Rhapsody in Blue" itself, with director Irving Rapper employing dreamy, abstract visuals that would later influence how Amadeus (1984) and The Music Lovers (1971) portrayed the creative process.

sections.content: The 1940s saw a wave of composer biopics that prioritized entertainment over accuracy. Song of Love (1947) took similar liberties with Robert Schumann's life story, while Words and Music (1948) glossed over Rodgers and Hart's complex relationship. These films established a template that later works like Coal Miner's Daughter (1980) and Walk the Line (2005) would both draw from and react against - the sanitized rise-fall-redemption arc that became standard in musical biopics.

What sets Rhapsody in Blue apart is its ambitious incorporation of classical music into a mainstream Hollywood framework. The film attempts to bridge high culture and popular entertainment much like Gershwin himself did. This influenced later classical music biopics like Song Without End (1960) about Franz Liszt and Lisztomania (1975), Ken Russell's wildly experimental take on the same composer. sections.content: Modern filmmaker approaches to musician biopics often explicitly reference or reject the conventions established in Rhapsody in Blue. Bohemian Rhapsody (2018) maintains the glossy approach while Love & Mercy (2014) deliberately deconstructs biopic tropes in its portrait of Brian Wilson. Amadeus (1984) particularly echoes Rapper's technique of visualizing musical composition through abstract imagery, though with far more psychological complexity.
